dataset_family: NACC Uniform Data Set (NIA-funded ADRCs, September 2005 to March 2017)
method_family: Automated FLAIR white-matter-hyperintensity segmentation with cross-sectional regression and longitudinal linear mixed-effects models of informant-rated NPI-Q severity scores
what_it_shows: The sample is 252 NACC participants: 114 with MCI due to AD and 138 with AD dementia, pooled and not stratified. At baseline, no NPI-Q severity score (the total or any of the 12 subscores, which include depression) was associated with whole-brain WMH load after FDR correction. Longitudinally, baseline WMH load was associated with an increase in the NPI-Q depression severity subscore in the mixed-effects model (p = .017). In the correlation plot of WMH against change in depression severity, however, r = 0.087 (p = 0.172).
why: PARTLY, in a different population. The baseline cross-sectional null fits the row's clause that severity scores fail to track brain measures. But (1) the sample pools MCI-AD with AD dementia and results are not given for the MCI group; (2) the brain measure is WMH, a small-vessel marker; (3) NPI-Q severity is an informant-rated 0-3 item score; and (4) the per-subscore cross-sectional results sit in supplementary Table S3, which is not in the extract. The main text states that none was significant. CUTS THE OTHER WAY: longitudinally, baseline WMH predicted worsening depression severity (mixed-effects p = .017). This is a brain measure tracking the course of depressive severity, which works against a dissociation between severity and neurobiology. Its strength is uncertain, because the correlation plot for depression change was not significant (r = 0.087, p = 0.172) and the Table 4 footnote states a one-tailed p < .10 significance convention. In the extract the '<' appears as ','; it was decoded from the paper's own notation, and the verdict does not depend on it. The study is therefore itself divided. It does not test the first clause (there is no non-impaired or non-depressed comparator) and has no conversion outcome. Excluding participants with a history of psychiatric disorders further restricts the depression range. INDEPENDENCE: NACC is not the dataset of any current supporter or other candidate, and no authors are shared (Anor, Dadar, Collins, Tartaglia; Toronto and Montreal). The ADNI template was used only for image registration.

quotes.quote: The final study cohort consisted of 252 participants (n = 114 with MCI-AD and n = 138 with AD).
Other exclusion criteria included history of seizures, psychiatric disorders, traumatic brain injury, stroke, other cognitive disorders, and primary etiologic diagnoses other than AD.

Cross-sectional analysis was performed to assess the association between baseline total NPS severity scores and baseline whole-brain WMH load. [...] In addition, the cross-sectional analysis was repeated for the 12 individual NPI severity scores. False discovery rate was used to correct for multiple comparisons.
The cross-sectional analysis at baseline revealed no significant association between any of the NPS scores (either total scores or subscores) and WMHs (see Table S3).

For the longitudinal mixed-effects model analyses of the NPS subscores, baseline WMH load was associated with significantly worse future NPI total scores (p = .014), delusions severity subscore (p = .023), hallucinations severity subscore (p = .040), agitation severity subscore (p = .093), depression severity subscore (p = .017), and irritability severity subscore (p = .002).
